overview.summary: Psychologists study how people think, feel and behave, and many help people with emotional or behavioural difficulties through assessment and talking therapies.
overview.problems: They help people understand themselves, cope with difficulties and improve their wellbeing, learning or work.
overview.worksWith: Clients or patients of all ages, families, teachers, doctors and other mental health professionals.
overview.workplaces: Clinics, hospitals, schools, universities, workplaces, research centres and private practice. The specialty, such as clinical, counselling, educational, organizational or research, changes the setting.

timeline.title: Prepare for sessions
timeline.description: The psychologist reads notes and plans each session.
timeline.why: Preparation helps make good use of limited time.

timeline.title: Sessions with clients
timeline.description: The psychologist listens carefully, asks questions and helps clients understand patterns and try new ways of coping. A session often lasts about an hour, though this varies.
timeline.why: A trusting relationship is central to being able to help.

timeline.title: Assessment and writing
timeline.description: The psychologist carries out structured assessments or questionnaires and writes reports that explain the results.
timeline.why: Careful assessment guides what kind of help is offered.

timeline.title: Supervision and team discussion
timeline.description: The psychologist discusses cases with a supervisor or colleagues, which is a normal part of professional practice.
timeline.why: Another point of view helps keep the work safe and ethical.

timeline.title: Records and follow-up
timeline.description: The psychologist writes confidential notes and arranges next steps.
timeline.why: Records support continuity of care and are protected by strict rules.

timeline.title: Research, teaching or consultation
timeline.description: Some psychologists study behaviour, teach, or advise schools and organizations.
timeline.why: Research and teaching keep the profession improving.

responsibilities: Providing support or therapy within their training
Staying up to date with research
challenges: Hearing painful stories can be emotionally heavy, so looking after yourself matters.
Progress with clients is often slow and uncertain.
Training is long, with study, supervised experience and, for clinical practice, often a postgraduate degree.
Strict ethical and legal duties, such as confidentiality, apply.
There is a lot of paperwork and record keeping.
Many services have waiting lists and limited resources.
It is important to be honest about what psychology can and cannot do.
workEnvironment: Quiet offices and consulting rooms, hospitals, schools or universities, usually with set appointments. Hours can include evenings in some roles. Research and organizational psychology are more office or laboratory based.
rewards: Helping people understand themselves and cope better
A mix of science and human contact
tradeoffs: Emotional demands and the need for self-care
A long and competitive training path
Results that can be slow to appear
Income and job availability that vary by country and specialty

activity.title: Practise careful, non-judgmental listening
steps: Ask a friend or family member who agrees to talk for five minutes about a recent happy or difficult school or work event.
Listen without interrupting or giving advice.
Then repeat back in your own words what you heard and ask one open question.
Ask them whether they felt listened to.
Note whether listening felt interesting or tiring.
activity.outcome: You practise active listening, which is a core skill in counselling and many other careers.
activity.safety: Talk only about everyday topics and do not push anyone to share things they find too private. Never try to diagnose or give mental health advice, and encourage anyone who is struggling to talk to a trusted adult or a qualified professional.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
